Acceptance criterion 1, HEAD/dirty tracked diff/relevant untracked state affect fingerprint: the digest is over the project's file contents, not over Git's diff, because a diff changes when the same files are committed, amended or rebased while the project state a check would read has not. HEAD is digested and the branch name is not -- the branch is recorded in GitState for a person to read, and two branches at the same commit are the same state. A deletion and an empty file are two states (the Gone arm writes a marker, not the digest of empty content). A clean project has no change digest at all, rather than the digest of an empty list, so clean and empty-list are two states and not one; the domain type says so with an Option and the code follows it. Acceptance criterion 2, fingerprint changes on relevant source changes: every change record contributes the file's own path and its contents, and the untracked tree is walked file by file. Digest framing: the domain tag sure.git-fingerprint.v1 is the first field, every field is written length-then-bytes so (ab,c) cannot hash equal to (a,bc), and an absent optional field writes a presence byte rather than an empty string. SHA-256, because the project being fingerprinted is written by a coding agent and an adversary choosing a collision is in scope, not hypothetical. Git is asked for status with --untracked-files=all --no-renames -- . plus a separate rev-parse --show-prefix. --relative is deliberately absent and is now forbidden by a comment and by a mutation: on this machine's Git 2.55.0.windows.3 it prints nothing at all for a repository with changes and exits 0, which is an empty change list indistinguishable from a clean tree -- a dirty project would have fingerprinted clean and every check keyed to it would have gone green. It was caught by a_dirty_project_fingerprints_differently_from_a_clean_one, not by reading the flag list. The prefix is stripped with Path::strip_prefix, not string comparison, so a project in app/ is not confused by a sibling app-old/. A nested checkout that Git reports as one untracked directory is walked and read; a walk that loses something is FingerprintError::IncompleteTree, never a hash of a partial tree; the byte budget is over the whole fingerprint and a file that crosses it is an error, never a prefix hash. ProjectFingerprint::matches compares kind and digest and never id. A tracked .gitattributes names a filter driver and the repository's own configuration gives it a command, so a plain git status executes it; measured with a marker program and a positive control, and it fires with nothing modified. Acceptance criterion 1, scoped content manifest is deterministic: the manifest is a SHA-256 over the walk's files and links, sorted by the text that goes into the digest rather than by the paths, with the path digested beside the contents so that a move or a name swap is a change. Two copies of one project in two directories agree (two_copies_of_one_project_are_one_fingerprint), which is what proves no absolute path reaches the digest. Every limit -- max_depth, max_entries, max_files, max_bytes -- is an error and never a digest over the part that fitted. Acceptance criterion 2, generated/vendor churn is excluded by documented rules: the walk IS crate::scan, the same tables and the same comparison the checks use, so the exclusion is not a second list that can drift. the_excluded_list_is_the_scans_and_not_a_second_copy_of_it pins the agreement rather than the list; churn_in_every_excluded_kind_of_directory_changes_nothing rewrites one directory per SkipReason (build output, vendored, caches, .venv, .sure) and asserts the digest does not move, with the control that a covered file does move it -- without that control a fingerprint that never moved at all would pass. a_repositorys_own_storage_is_out_so_a_commit_does_not_move_the_manifest makes an empty commit, asserts the ref really moved, and then asserts the manifest did not. The decision this task owned, and it is the reason choose.rs exists rather than a boolean in a caller: a project is fingerprinted by Git when it is at the ROOT of the working tree containing it, not merely inside one. rev-parse --show-prefix is empty exactly then. A directory one level inside somebody else's checkout gets Content, because the Git kind would digest the OUTER repository's HEAD -- a commit anywhere else in that repository moves the subdirectory's fingerprint although not one of its files changed, and evidence marked stale for a project nobody touched is how a person learns to ignore the word. That is measured, both ways, in the_git_kind_moves_for_a_commit_the_project_is_not_part_of_and_the_content_kind_does_not, which also asserts the Git kind still DOES move, so the reason cannot quietly become folklore. P2-T009.notes:
P2-T009 — implement README/spec command and claim extraction.

Acceptance: "Extracted commands are untrusted documentation and never
auto-executed merely because documented."

DELIVERED. `sure_core::documents` (crates/sure-core/src/documents.rs): a
`DocumentReport::of(&Discovery)` that finds the project's documents, reads each
one's fenced code blocks, and returns a `DocumentedCommand` per command line —
carrying the text as one string, the shell family the fence named, whether a
prompt marker was removed, the heading it sits under, the document and the
1-based line. Plus crates/sure-core/tests/document_commands.rs (20 tests).

The acceptance's first half is a label: every command reaches the intent model
as `IntentSource::ProjectSpec`, *derived* from `Config::goal_source()` rather
than restated, so a project file is documentation here for the same reason it is
documentation in `support::classify`, and there is still one place that decides
it. A `DocumentedCommand` is the claim and there is one list rather than two: a
fenced block carrying a language is the only claim a document makes that SURE
can read off by rule, and pulling requirements out of a sentence would be the
T17 hallucination. `lying-readme`'s description ("README setup command does not
work on fixture") and `P4-T005`'s acceptance both read it that way.

The second half is about something that did not happen, which is the kind of
claim that is easy to write and hard to hold. It is held by asserting three
things together — the command was found, the document was read, and a recursive
snapshot of the project is byte-identical before and after — with a control
proving the snapshot helper can see a new file, because a helper that never
notices anything would satisfy the first assertion perfectly. The fixture's
command is `npm install && echo SURE-RAN-THIS > SURE-RAN-THIS.txt`, so the
evidence of a leak is a file whose absence is checkable rather than an inference.

"Never auto-executed" is a property of the shape rather than a promise. No field
on `DocumentedCommand` can hold a program and its arguments, no shell-splitting
exists anywhere in `sure-core`'s shipped code, `DocumentReport::of` is the only
door a report can come through, and `sure-cli` builds no `DocumentReport` at
all. The module declines the stronger claim in as many words: there is no
function that turns a `DocumentedCommand` into an `ApprovedCommand`, so the path
does not exist rather than being blocked.

Indentation is ignored when looking for a fence, and that is the one deliberate
departure from CommonMark: a fence inside a list item is indented by the marker
width, so following the spec exactly reports no commands *and* a complete
reading, which is a silent loss dressed as a clean result.

P2-T011 — implement intent source tracking (provenance/trust labels).

Acceptance: "Intent sources preserve provenance/trust labels." and "Inferred
intent cannot satisfy user requirements."

DELIVERED. `sure_core::intent_model` (crates/sure-core/src/intent_model.rs, 14
unit tests) and crates/sure-core/tests/intent_sources.rs (7 tests), plus
`pub mod intent_model;` in lib.rs and a corrected PROJECT_INTENT.md.

The acceptance's first sentence is a claim about a label *surviving*, and a test
can hold it wrongly by reading the label off and agreeing with it. So every test
that asserts a label here also drives the statement through
`may_claim_full_fulfilment`, which is the gate the label is actually for. The
second sentence is held by driving an intent of nothing but guesses through the
same gate and asserting it cannot reach zero requirements short.

THE SHAPE, which is the whole design. Every channel has a **door**: a function
that produces a `Requirement` and writes its own `IntentSource`. No function here
that produces a `Requirement` takes an `IntentSource` as an argument, so a caller
holding a command it read out of a README has nothing to ask for — there is no
parameter to ask with. Provenance survives by a shape the module does not offer
an alternative to, rather than by a rule its code follows. The one function that
does take a source, `from_source`, goes the other way: it reads statements *back*
by the label they arrived with, and the module comment names it rather than
leaving a reader to find it and doubt the rule.

`observed_user_request` takes an `&Authority` and not a `&Config`, and the same
bytes on disk give opposite answers. `sure.yaml` lives inside the project, and
the project is written by the same agent whose work is being judged, so
`privacy.full_recording: true` there is a **request**;
`Authority::privilege(ProjectRequest::FullRecording)` is asked whether anyone was
able to grant it, and only the user's own settings outside the project can. The
integration test holds one `sure.yaml`, byte for byte, refused first as an
escalation and then granted — with a control asserting the kept request is worth
exactly what a goal that was typed is worth, because the privacy decision is
about whether the words are kept and not about how much they count.

`DocumentReport::as_requirements` are one channel reached by two doors, and both
ask `Config::goal_source()` rather than naming the label themselves, so P2-T009's
decision point is still the only one. `documented_goal` answers `None` for a goal
with no words rather than manufacturing a blank requirement, and it keeps the
project's own spacing — the test feeds it a padded goal, because a door that
tidied the words and still set `raw_retained` would be reporting something it did
not do. `agent_claim` and `inferred` leave `raw_retained` false: the claim door
does not know whether the caller kept the agent's sentence or restated it, and an
inference has no original wording behind it at all.

The working directory was covered, in the one position the operating system takes

turned into a command line by somebody; an **argument**; a value in the
**environment block**, a second encoding surface with its own conversion; and, in

space and a character outside ASCII" means one thing everywhere it is used.
`NOT_ASCII` carries three different problems rather than one, because the three
fail differently: `é` is what a byte-oriented path passes through and a code-page
conversion does not, `中文` is what only a real encoding survives, and `🎉` is
outside the Basic Multilingual Plane — two UTF-16 code units, one surrogate pair
— which is the case a conversion that stops at the first unit truncates.

THE TREE TEST'S CENTRAL ASSERTION PROVED NOTHING ON WINDOWS, AND THAT WAS
MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED. Its claim is "a stop reaches the whole tree" and its
evidence was that the grandchild's report never appeared — but **a file that is
absent is what a stopped grandchild leaves behind and also what a grandchild that
never ran leaves behind**. Measured twice on this machine: with the grandchild's
mode string changed to a name that is not a test, and the new marker assertion in
place, the test fails saying the grandchild never started; with that assertion
removed — the old reading — the same run passes, in 3.26s, reporting `WholeTree`
about a tree that never existed. On Unix the same change fails loudly, because
that branch asserts the opposite outcome, so the hole was in the branch that
skipped a measurement.

The fix is a positive control. `child_waits_to_be_released` writes
`<report>.started` the moment it is running and then waits for `<report>.release`;
the parent asserts the marker **before** it reads the absence, so "the stop
reached it" and "it never existed" can no longer be confused, and afterwards it
drops the release to ask the second question by the only means both platforms
have — a process that is running writes within a poll and a process that was
stopped cannot write at all. Waiting on a file instead of sleeping also takes the
clock out of the test: the old grandchild slept 1.5s, which must be long enough
not to finish before the stop and short enough to be worth waiting out, and on a
fast machine the first of those is what breaks.
`a_cancelled_run_reaches_what_it_started_too` holds the same claim for the
caller's decision rather than the runner's clock, cancelling only after the marker
exists so the test cannot race two process starts.

set of categories the command *may* fall into — plus a `Source` saying why. The
five categories live in the domain beside the permissions they already answer
with: `CommandClass`, one wire name each, and `CommandEffects` as a canonical set
with `union`, `contains`, `is_static_only` and a `ungrantable()` door. One commit,
`967c5e6`, five files: `crates/sure-domain/src/execution.rs` +414,
`crates/sure-core/src/safety.rs` +1278, `crates/sure-core/tests/command_safety.rs`

THE ACCEPTANCE SENTENCE IS SATISFIED BY CONSTRUCTION AND BY TEST, AND THE TWO ARE
NOT THE SAME CLAIM. Distinctness by construction is the enum and its frozen wire
names; distinctness as a fact about behaviour is a test that takes **every ordered
pair of the five** and shows a command can be told apart under one from under the
other, over a witness table with one single-category command per category. The
witnesses are `git status`, `npm test`, `cargo add serde --offline`, `git fetch`
and `git reset --hard`, and the test asserts the witness table is as long as
`CommandClass::ALL` — so a sixth category with no witness fails the test rather
than passing quietly. `rustc` cannot tell a category apart from a category, and
that is the gap those tests close.

**THE ONE RULE THE MODULE IS ARRANGED AROUND: nothing is `Static` unless a rule in
the file says so.** A program with no row, a known program with an operation the
table has no name for, and a command line whose meaning is in text SURE cannot
read all come back as *every category but `Static`*. That is the only mistake here
that nothing downstream could catch, and it is held by a test named for the
sentence — `nothing_sure_could_not_read_is_ever_static` — which walks the unknown
programs, the unknown operations and the four wrappers. A fourth cause is handled
the same way and is easy to miss: an argument that is not text SURE can read makes
the whole line unread rather than being dropped, because dropping one token from
`git <bytes> status` would leave SURE reading the `status` behind the bytes and
answering `Static` about a command line it did not read.

**`Destructive` HAS NO PERMISSION THAT COVERS IT, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.**
`required_permission()` answers `None` for it. `WriteProject` is writing *inside*
the project, which `rm -rf ..\..\` is not, and `git push --force` is not a write at
all; folding it in would let a consent to write a file read as a consent to
destroy the machine. `ungrantable()` is the door a caller uses to find that out,
and a test holds it. What *should* cover it is `P3-T005`'s question, and answering
it here would have put a permission decision inside the classifier.

**ONE CORRECTION DURING THE WORK, AGAINST MY OWN FIRST TABLE.** `python -m pip
install` was filed as `Install` alone and an integration test caught it: the
domain's `ActionKind::InstallDependencies` has `executes_project_code()` true and
`can_touch_network()` true, because a source distribution is built by a build
backend the package brought with it and npm runs lifecycle scripts. The domain was
the authority; the table was wrong. Everything that may run a package's own
install steps is `INSTALLS_AND_RUNS`; `RESOLVES` is what cargo's manifest-only
operations get. That integration test walks the command set SURE's own discovery
builds — `cargo test`, `npm test`, `npm run build`, `python -m pytest`,
`python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`, `uv sync`, `poetry run pytest` — so a
change that stops classifying one of them fails rather than going unnoticed.

**THE VOCABULARY GAP IS STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER.** The acceptance names
five categories and none of them is "changes files in this directory without
destroying anything". `git commit` and `git branch -m` are therefore
`UnknownOperation` — not `Static`, and not a sixth class invented here, which
would have made the acceptance sentence untrue by satisfying it. `git pull` *is*
classified, because one of its effects is one the vocabulary has. `git branch`,
`tag`, `config`, `remote`, `stash`, `cargo clean` and `npm audit` are absent on
the rule the module writes down: a verb is in the table only when every form SURE
can name has an effect SURE can name.
